newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel backs reduced test for Novartis clozaril.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel backs reduced test for Novartis clozaril.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration advisory panel on Monday recommended reducing the frequency of blood monitoring for schizophrenics taking Novartis Pharmaceuticals Corp's clozapine (clozaril).
The panel said tests could be done bi-weekly after six months of therapy, and that after a year, testing could become voluntary. The final decision will be worked out by Novartis and the FDA.

Clozaril patients have been required to have a weekly white blood cell count as long as they are on the drug, as they risk developing a fatal condition called agranulocytosis. The drug is for those who fail to respond to other schizophrenia therapies and sales run about $500 million a year.
Patient advocates sought less testing, claiming that the weekly blood draw is a hurdle to starting therapy, inconvenient, and often leads to collapsed veins and discontinuation.
Novartis cautioned against reduced testing, saying it will lead to more agranulocytosis and more deaths.
Despite the panel's recommendation, Novartis does not expect reduced testing to increase the number of patients on the drug, as they would still have weekly testing in the first six months.
At least 150,000 patients have taken Clozaril since its launch in 1990. Novartis analyzed data from 67,600 patients in the Clozaril National Registry from 1990 through April 1995.
The risk of developing agranulocytosis is highest in the first six months and declines with longer use, although the risk still exists at any time.
"There is a need to continue monitoring long term," said Ravi Anand, a researcher at Novartis. Some patients have developed agranulocytosis as long as three years after starting therapy, he said.
During the five years, 400 patients developed agranulocytosis, and 12 died from the condition. About 340 cases occurred in the first six months, as did all deaths.

The mortality rate is at least 3 percent, and may be as high as 15 percent, said Noel Weiss, a University of Washington epidemiologist who represented Novartis. The overall risk of developing agranulocytosis is 2.5 cases per 1,000 people, said Weiss.

FDA reviewer Judith Racoosin called that estimate "conservative." Even with the worst case scenario -- patients receive no testing and all those who develop low white blood cell counts went on to get agranulocytosis -- the rate would be five cases per 1,000, she said. That is within range of rates seen in other marketed drugs, which do not require blood monitoring, said Racoosin.
